label: A mathematical story from 1900
title: Hilbert sets 23 challenges for a new century
explanation: David Hilbert published a list of 23 problems intended to guide twentieth-century mathematics and presented a selection of them at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Paris. Some were precise questions and others were broad research programmes; several remain open today.
whyItMatters: The list helped organise mathematical research and connected generations of mathematicians through a shared set of difficult questions.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1900–1910 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1901
title: Russell finds a paradox inside unrestricted sets
explanation: Bertrand Russell noticed that allowing any description to define a set leads to a contradiction. Asking whether 'the set of all sets that do not contain themselves' contains itself produces opposite answers at once.
whyItMatters: Russell's paradox showed that set theory needed carefully stated axioms rather than an unrestricted rule for building sets.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1900–1910 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1902
title: Lebesgue enlarges the meaning of area
explanation: Henri Lebesgue defined a new integral by grouping points according to the values a function takes, rather than only cutting its input interval into thin strips. His method can measure and integrate many functions that older methods cannot handle.
whyItMatters: The Lebesgue integral became a foundation for modern analysis, probability and the mathematics of signals.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1900–1910 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1903
title: Fredholm turns integral equations into a theory
explanation: Ivar Fredholm published a general method for a major class of equations in which the unknown function appears inside an integral. He used determinants and convergent series to explain when solutions exist and how they can be represented.
whyItMatters: Fredholm's work helped begin operator theory, a language now used across differential equations, quantum mechanics and numerical analysis.
sourceTitle: Sur une classe d'équations fonctionnelles — Acta Mathematica

label: A mathematical story from 1904
title: Poincaré asks how to recognise a three-sphere
explanation: Henri Poincaré asked whether every closed three-dimensional space with no essential loops must be the three-dimensional analogue of a sphere. The statement became the Poincaré conjecture and was finally proved nearly a century later.
whyItMatters: The question became a central test of how local information about loops can reveal the global shape of a space.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1900–1910 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1905
title: Complicated polynomial ideals gain building blocks
explanation: Emanuel Lasker proved that ideals in polynomial rings can be broken into primary pieces, rather as an integer can be analysed through prime-power pieces. Emmy Noether later extended and clarified the result in a much broader setting.
whyItMatters: Primary decomposition gives algebraists a structured way to study systems of polynomial equations and the geometric shapes they describe.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1900–1910 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1906
title: A simple curve grows to infinite length
explanation: Helge von Koch's 1906 paper developed an elementary geometric construction of a continuous curve that has no tangent anywhere. Replacing every line segment with a repeating four-segment zigzag makes the length grow without limit even though the curve remains inside a bounded region.
whyItMatters: The Koch curve made strange infinite behaviour visible and later became a classic example of fractal geometry.
sourceTitle: Une méthode géométrique élémentaire pour l'étude de certaines questions de la théorie des courbes planes — Acta Mathematica

label: A mathematical story from 1907
title: Topology learns to build spaces from pieces
explanation: Poul Heegaard and Max Dehn published Analysis Situs, which organised methods for studying spaces by dividing them into combinatorial pieces. Instead of depending on exact lengths and angles, these methods track how vertices, edges, faces and higher-dimensional pieces connect.
whyItMatters: Their work helped establish combinatorial topology, where discrete structures reveal properties of continuous shapes.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1900–1910 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1908
title: Small samples get a reliable statistical test
people: William Sealy Gosset, writing as Student
explanation: William Sealy Gosset introduced Student's t-distribution and t-test while studying small batches of data at a brewery. The method adjusts for the extra uncertainty that appears when a population's spread must be estimated from only a few observations.
whyItMatters: The t-test made careful comparisons possible in small experiments and remains one of the most widely taught statistical tools.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1900–1910 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1909
title: Analytic number theory receives a systematic map
explanation: Edmund Landau published a major systematic account of analytic number theory, the study of whole numbers using tools from calculus and complex analysis. It gathered rigorous results about how prime numbers are distributed and gave researchers a shared reference.
whyItMatters: Landau's work helped turn scattered techniques into a coherent field for investigating the hidden patterns of primes.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1900–1910 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1910
title: Principia Mathematica rebuilds mathematics in logic
people: Alfred North Whitehead and Bertrand Russell
explanation: Whitehead and Russell published the first volume of Principia Mathematica, an enormous attempt to derive mathematics from explicitly stated logical rules. Its symbolic proofs showed how even familiar arithmetic could be unpacked into many tiny reasoning steps.
whyItMatters: The project shaped modern logic and sharpened questions about what formal systems can and cannot prove.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1910–1920 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1911
title: Polynomials learn to imitate any continuous curve
explanation: Sergei Bernstein gave a constructive proof that a continuous function on a closed interval can be approximated as closely as desired by polynomials. His Bernstein polynomials use probability-like weights to blend sampled values of the function.
whyItMatters: The proof supplies an explicit approximation recipe and links analysis, probability and modern curve design.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1910–1920 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1912
title: Integration reaches beyond Lebesgue's boundary
explanation: Arnaud Denjoy introduced an extended integral designed to recover a function from a much wider class of derivatives. It can integrate certain highly irregular functions that are not Lebesgue-integrable.
whyItMatters: The Denjoy integral clarified how far the fundamental connection between differentiation and integration can be extended.
sourceTitle: Denjoy integral — Encyclopedia of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1913
title: Ramanujan's letter crosses two mathematical worlds
people: Srinivasa Ramanujan and G. H. Hardy
explanation: Srinivasa Ramanujan sent G. H. Hardy a letter filled with striking formulas about infinite series, continued fractions and number theory. Hardy recognised extraordinary originality, and their later collaboration brought many of Ramanujan's discoveries into rigorous published mathematics.
whyItMatters: The correspondence began one of mathematics' most remarkable partnerships and revealed ideas that still inspire research.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1910–1920 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1914
title: Hausdorff gives abstract spaces a rulebook
explanation: Felix Hausdorff published Grundzüge der Mengenlehre, developing a systematic theory of metric and topological spaces. His separation condition explains when two distinct points can be enclosed in non-overlapping neighbourhoods.
whyItMatters: The book helped make topology an independent subject and supplied language used throughout modern geometry and analysis.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1910–1920 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1915
title: A triangle repeats itself at every scale
explanation: Wacław Sierpiński rigorously described the recursive triangular curve now called the Sierpiński triangle. Remove the middle quarter from a triangle, repeat the same removal in the three remaining triangles, and a self-similar pattern appears at every scale.
whyItMatters: The construction became an accessible doorway to recursion, topology and the later theory of fractals.
sourceTitle: Sierpiński's curve: a beautiful paradigm of recursion — Roma Tre University

label: A mathematical story from 1916
title: One explicit number is normal in every base
explanation: Sierpiński constructed the first explicit absolutely normal number: a number whose digits are evenly distributed not just in base ten, but in every integer base greater than one. Almost every real number has this property in a probability sense, yet writing down a proven example was difficult.
whyItMatters: The result exposed the gap between proving that objects are plentiful and giving a concrete formula for one of them.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1910–1920 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1917
title: How little space can a turning needle use?
explanation: Sōichi Kakeya posed a problem asking for the smallest-area region in which a unit line segment can turn through every direction. Surprisingly, later constructions showed that needle sets can have arbitrarily small area, leading to deeper questions about their dimension.
whyItMatters: The simple moving-needle puzzle grew into a major subject connecting geometry, waves and Fourier analysis.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1910–1920 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1918
title: Every continuous symmetry carries a conservation law
explanation: Emmy Noether published two theorems linking continuous symmetries of a mathematical model to conserved quantities. For example, if the rules do not change with time, the corresponding system conserves energy.
whyItMatters: Noether's theorem created a deep bridge between abstract symmetry and the equations used throughout modern physics.
field: Mathematical physics and calculus of variations
sourceTitle: A Century of Noether's Theorem — arXiv

label: A mathematical story from 1919
title: Dimension is no longer forced to be a whole number
explanation: Felix Hausdorff introduced a way to assign dimension using how measurements change with scale. A rough set can therefore have a dimension such as 1.26, lying between an ordinary line and an ordinary surface.
whyItMatters: Hausdorff dimension gives mathematicians a precise tool for comparing fractals and other irregular sets.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1910–1920 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1920
title: Takagi builds the foundations of class field theory
explanation: Teiji Takagi published the paper that established the central existence theorem of class field theory. It linked certain extensions of a number field to structured groups built from its ideals, turning patterns of prime-number splitting into an organised theory.
whyItMatters: Takagi's work unified earlier reciprocity laws and supplied a foundation for twentieth-century algebraic number theory.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1920–1930 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1921
title: Noether gives abstract algebra a stopping rule
explanation: In Idealtheorie in Ringbereichen, Emmy Noether showed how an ascending-chain condition makes ideals in a ring manageable and supports decomposition theorems. Rings satisfying this condition are now called Noetherian rings.
whyItMatters: Her structural viewpoint replaced long calculations with general concepts and reshaped modern algebra.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1920–1930 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1922
title: Weather forecasting becomes a numerical calculation
explanation: Lewis Fry Richardson published a method for predicting weather by dividing the atmosphere into a grid and repeatedly solving equations for each part. His hand calculation was impractical and inaccurate, but the mathematical plan anticipated computer weather models.
whyItMatters: The project showed how differential equations and numerical methods could turn physical laws into forecasts.
sourceTitle: Richardson's Fantastic Forecast Factory — European Meteorological Society

label: A mathematical story from 1923
title: Artin invents new functions for hidden number symmetries
explanation: Emil Artin introduced L-functions that package information about the symmetries of extensions of number systems. He also made a still-important conjecture predicting when these functions have no unwanted singularities.
whyItMatters: Artin L-functions became central objects in number theory and later formed part of the vast Langlands programme.
sourceTitle: On the history of Artin's L-functions — Heidelberg University

label: A mathematical story from 1924
title: A sphere grows interlocking horns
explanation: James Alexander constructed the horned sphere, a surface formed by repeatedly growing pairs of linked, narrowing horns. The surface itself is topologically a sphere, but the space outside it behaves very differently from the outside of an ordinary round sphere.
whyItMatters: The example proved that familiar-looking topological statements can fail when objects are embedded in wild ways.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1920–1930 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1925
title: Experiments receive a practical statistical toolkit
explanation: Ronald Fisher published Statistical Methods for Research Workers, explaining practical tools for drawing conclusions from experimental data. The book helped spread significance tests, analysis of variance and careful attention to experimental uncertainty.
whyItMatters: It changed how researchers in biology and many other subjects designed experiments and judged evidence.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1920–1930 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1926
title: A cube becomes a one-dimensional sponge
explanation: Karl Menger described the Menger sponge while studying mathematical dimension. Repeatedly divide a cube into 27 smaller cubes and remove the centre and six face-centres; the limiting object has zero volume yet an endlessly intricate structure with topological dimension one.
whyItMatters: The sponge makes recursion and competing ideas of dimension visible in a single memorable object.
sourceTitle: The maths inside the Menger sponge — London Mathematical Society

label: A mathematical story from 1927
title: Artin proves a universal reciprocity law
explanation: Emil Artin proved his general reciprocity law, a theorem describing how prime numbers split when one number system is enlarged. It unified several older reciprocity laws that had previously looked like separate patterns.
whyItMatters: Artin reciprocity became a foundation of class field theory and a model for deeper links between symmetry and primes.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1920–1930 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1928
title: Two-player strategy games find a balance
explanation: John von Neumann proved the minimax theorem for finite two-player zero-sum games. It says the best guaranteed outcome for one player equals the worst outcome the opponent can force when both may mix their strategies randomly.
whyItMatters: The theorem put strategic decision-making on a rigorous mathematical foundation and launched modern game theory.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1920–1930 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1929
title: First-order logic is proved complete
explanation: In his doctoral dissertation, Kurt Gödel proved the completeness theorem for first-order logic. It says that any statement true in every interpretation of a set of logical assumptions can be derived using the formal proof rules.
whyItMatters: The theorem showed a precise agreement between semantic truth and formal proof for first-order logic.
sourceTitle: Kurt Gödel — Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

label: A mathematical story from 1930
title: Two forbidden networks explain every crossing
explanation: Kazimierz Kuratowski characterised exactly which finite networks can be drawn on a flat sheet without crossing edges. A graph is non-planar precisely when it contains a subdivided version of one of two basic obstructions, K₅ or K₃,₃.
whyItMatters: A potentially endless drawing problem was reduced to recognising two fundamental patterns.
sourceTitle: The theorem on planar graphs — Historia Mathematica

label: A mathematical story from 1931
title: Formal arithmetic meets an unavoidable limit
explanation: Kurt Gödel proved that any consistent, effectively described formal system strong enough for basic arithmetic contains statements it can neither prove nor disprove. He also showed that such a system cannot prove its own consistency under the theorem's standard assumptions.
whyItMatters: The incompleteness theorems established permanent limits on what one fixed list of axioms can settle.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1930–1940 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1932
title: Quantum mechanics receives a Hilbert-space framework
explanation: John von Neumann published Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics, expressing quantum states as vectors in Hilbert space and measurable quantities as operators. The book separated the mathematical rules from any one physical example and treated measurement with unusual precision.
whyItMatters: Its operator-based framework became a standard mathematical language for quantum theory and functional analysis.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1930–1940 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1933
title: Probability receives three clear axioms
explanation: Andrey Kolmogorov presented probability as a measure on a collection of events, governed by three axioms. The framework says probabilities are non-negative, the whole sample space has probability one, and mutually exclusive events add appropriately.
whyItMatters: These axioms gave probability a rigorous foundation flexible enough for both simple games and complex random processes.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1930–1940 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1934
title: An irrational power is proved transcendental
explanation: Working independently, Gelfond and Schneider proved that aᵇ is transcendental when a is algebraic but not 0 or 1 and b is an irrational algebraic number. This settled Hilbert's seventh problem and proves, for example, that 2 to the power √2 is transcendental.
whyItMatters: The theorem distinguishes numbers that cannot satisfy any polynomial equation with integer coefficients.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1930–1940 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1935
title: A counting rule guarantees a perfect matching
explanation: Philip Hall proved a precise condition for choosing a different representative from every set in a collection. In its famous matching form, every person in one group can be paired with an acceptable partner exactly when every subgroup collectively knows at least as many possible partners as the subgroup contains.
whyItMatters: Hall's marriage theorem became a fundamental test for matchings in combinatorics, networks and assignment problems.
sourceTitle: On Representatives of Subsets — Journal of the London Mathematical Society

label: A mathematical story from 1936
title: A paper machine defines what an algorithm can do
explanation: Alan Turing described an idealised machine that reads and writes symbols on an unlimited tape according to a finite table of rules. He used it to show that no single algorithm can decide whether every possible program will eventually halt.
whyItMatters: The Turing machine supplied a precise mathematical model of general computation and exposed its fundamental limits.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1930–1940 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1937
title: Large odd numbers become sums of three primes
explanation: Ivan Vinogradov proved that every sufficiently large odd integer can be written as the sum of three prime numbers. His theorem did not cover every smaller odd number, but it was a decisive advance toward the weak Goldbach conjecture.
whyItMatters: The proof showed that analytic estimates can control how prime numbers combine additively.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1930–1940 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1938
title: Random motion gains an analytic foundation
explanation: Kolmogorov published Analytic Methods in Probability Theory, developing equations that describe how transition probabilities evolve in Markov processes. In a Markov process, the next step depends on the present state rather than the complete path used to reach it.
whyItMatters: The work became a foundation for modelling changing random systems in physics, biology, finance and computing.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1930–1940 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1939
title: Minimal surfaces learn to carry holes
explanation: Jesse Douglas extended his earlier work on Plateau's problem to minimal surfaces with more complicated topology, including prescribed numbers of holes and boundary curves. Instead of asking only for a disk-like soap film across one loop, the mathematics could now control the type of surface being spanned.
whyItMatters: The 1939 work broadened the rigorous theory of minimal surfaces beyond the simplest boundary-and-disk setting.
field: Geometric analysis and calculus of variations
sourceTitle: The higher topological form of Plateau's problem — Annali della Scuola Normale Superiore di Pisa

label: A mathematical story from 1940
title: Gödel constructs a universe where choice is consistent
explanation: Kurt Gödel published a detailed construction of an inner universe of sets in which both the axiom of choice and the generalized continuum hypothesis hold. Therefore, if the usual Zermelo–Fraenkel axioms are consistent, adding those two statements does not create a contradiction.
whyItMatters: The work introduced the constructible universe and proved one half of the later independence result for the continuum hypothesis.
sourceTitle: The Consistency of the Axiom of Choice and of the Generalized Continuum-Hypothesis — Princeton University Press

label: A mathematical story from 1941
title: The large sieve filters number patterns at once
explanation: Yuri Linnik introduced the large sieve, a method for bounding a set of integers by checking how its members are distributed across many remainder classes. Unlike a physical sieve that removes one kind of multiple at a time, this inequality controls many modular restrictions together.
whyItMatters: The large sieve became a versatile tool for studying primes and other thin sets of integers.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1940–1950 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1942
title: New operations detect twists in spaces
explanation: Norman Steenrod introduced the first Steenrod squares, operations that transform cohomology classes of a topological space into new ones. These operations can distinguish spaces whose simpler measurements look identical.
whyItMatters: Steenrod operations gave algebraic topologists powerful new tests for the hidden structure of high-dimensional spaces.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1940–1950 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1943
title: Abstract operator algebras find a concrete home
explanation: Gelfand and Naimark proved that every abstract C*-algebra can be represented as an algebra of bounded operators on a Hilbert space. The theorem connects a list of algebraic and geometric rules to concrete transformations of vectors.
whyItMatters: Their result made C*-algebras a central language for operator theory and the mathematical foundations of quantum mechanics.
sourceTitle: On the imbedding of normed rings into the ring of operators in Hilbert space — Mat. Sbornik

label: A mathematical story from 1944
title: Game theory enters economics
people: John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern
explanation: Von Neumann and Morgenstern published Theory of Games and Economic Behavior, using mathematics to study decisions in which each participant's outcome depends on everyone else's choices. The book developed strategic games and an axiomatic theory of utility.
whyItMatters: It established game theory as a systematic subject with applications in economics, politics, biology and computer science.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1940–1950 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1945
title: Categories describe mathematics through relationships
people: Samuel Eilenberg and Saunders Mac Lane
explanation: Eilenberg and Mac Lane introduced the terms category and natural transformation. A category focuses on mathematical objects and the structure-preserving maps between them, while a natural transformation compares whole families of such maps.
whyItMatters: Category theory became a unifying language for expressing the same structural pattern across different areas of mathematics.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1940–1950 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1946
title: Algebraic geometry is rebuilt without coordinates
explanation: André Weil published Foundations of Algebraic Geometry, giving an abstract and rigorous framework for studying shapes defined by polynomial equations. His approach handled varieties over many different fields rather than relying only on complex-number coordinates.
whyItMatters: The book helped prepare algebraic geometry for its powerful modern reformulation and wider links to number theory.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1940–1950 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1947
title: The simplex method walks toward the best answer
explanation: George Dantzig devised the simplex method for optimising a linear objective under linear constraints. Geometrically, it moves along corners of a many-dimensional feasible shape until no neighbouring corner improves the answer.
whyItMatters: The method made large planning and allocation problems practically solvable and launched modern linear programming.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1940–1950 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1948
title: Information becomes a measurable quantity
explanation: Claude Shannon published a mathematical theory of communication in which information is measured in bits and uncertainty is quantified by entropy. He proved limits on how efficiently messages can be compressed and how reliably they can cross a noisy channel.
whyItMatters: Information theory underlies digital communication, data compression, error correction and much of modern computing.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1940–1950 — MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1949
title: Weil predicts a hidden geometry over finite fields
explanation: André Weil stated a set of conjectures about counting solutions to polynomial equations over finite fields. They predicted that the resulting counting formula behaves like the topology of a geometric shape and includes an analogue of the Riemann hypothesis.
whyItMatters: The Weil conjectures drove the creation of major new tools in algebraic geometry and were eventually proved over the following decades.
sourceTitle: Numbers of solutions of equations in finite fields — Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society
